title: How Accurately Can a Gaussian Approximate Stochastic Approximation Iterates?
claim: A time-varying Gaussian tracks finite-time iterate distributions closely at all times, while the asymptotic limit is accurate only after many steps.
layout: 2x3 grid of histogram panels, columns by increasing k, rows by step-size
description: Six histogram panels in a 2x3 grid. The top row has step-size parameter ξ=0.8 and the bottom row has ξ=0.9. Columns show increasing iteration counts k=100, 1000 and 5000, labeled (a) to (f) beneath each panel. Each panel plots density against y_k as blue histogram bars. A black dashed curve shows the asymptotic Gaussian, and a red dashed curve shows the time-varying Gaussian. The red curve overlaps the histogram in every panel. The black curve fits poorly at small k: it is clearly too narrow and tall in panel (d), and slightly too tall in (a). It converges to the red curve and the histogram as k grows. Each panel has a legend in the upper right. The eye goes first to panel (d), where the mismatch is largest.
caption: Comparing the Gaussian approximations for $y_k$ at various time instants.
abstract: Stochastic approximation (SA) is a method for finding the root of an operator perturbed by noise. The focus of this paper is studying the distribution of SA iterates in finite time. In general, it is not possible to characterize the exact distribution, and therefore our goal is to find an approximation which can yield useful tail bounds. Inspired by the rich literature on the asymptotic normality of rescaled SA iterates, we approximate the pre-limit distributions by a sequence of Gaussians whose covariance is recursively defined. In particular, we establish explicit bounds on the Wasserstein-1 distance between the rescaled iterate at time $k$ and the aforementioned Gaussian for various choices of step-sizes. Since these covariances converge to the classical asymptotic limit, our analysis also provides a convergence rate for asymptotic normality as a by-product. As an immediate consequence of our bounds, we obtain tail bounds on the error of SA iterates at any time. Finally, we establish the sharpness of our rates by providing matching lower bounds and validate our findings through simulations. We obtain the sharp rates by first studying the convergence rate of the discrete Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (O-U) process driven by general noise, whose stationary distribution is identical to the limiting Gaussian distribution of the rescaled SA iterates. We believe that this is of independent interest, given its connection to sampling literature. The analysis involves adapting Stein's method for Gaussian approximation to handle the matrix weighted sum of i.i.d. random variables. The desired finite-time bounds for SA are obtained by characterizing the error dynamics between the rescaled SA iterate and the discrete time O-U process and combining it with the convergence rate of the latter process.
